The distinction between truly free to play and pay to win games is really simple: "Does this game allow me to spend money for an in-game advantage?" If yes, no matter how small, it's p2w. If no, and there is no cost to buying the game, then it's f2p. I think Dota2 and TF2 are good examples of how you can still make tons of money on cosmetic items that the community develops for the game. It's like monetizing modders, but the modders get a cut of the profits as well.

Even if the p2w elements are initially not very intrusive in a game, developers over time get greedy and will increase them until you have to pay to keep up, so definitely stay away from those. Mobile games & chinese seem to be more upfront about charging you tons of money, and if you're not a whale in those you're just fishfood for the whale's entertainment.

Western audiences seem to dislike p2w more than eastern audiences, so they have to disguise it more for western audiences. Some games that I have enjoyed that are "f2p" but are actually p2w would be stuff like Black Desert Online, World of Warships, etc. They lure players in with a sense that they can just grind a little extra to get whatever the p2w player has, but it's not really true. Technically speaking you can grind to get to the same point as the whales, but it requires an inordinate amount of time. World of Warships has a lot more skill and positioning so you can still have fun and contribute, but I'd hate to be grinding out upgrades. League of Legends reminds me of this as well, where you have to buy new heroes and upgrading them takes forever or $$. This seems to be one avenue that game developers are using to trick consumers into investing time and money into a game. To me it's a major detriment to games, because they are purposefully inserting unfun and time-gated mechanics to milk consumers out of money. I would rather go back to paying $60 once and getting a fun gaming experience, or even paying a subscription to online games to support server infrastructure than to have all games be gated behind either time sinks or cash sinks.
